about: Agency-requisition templates for a cyber crisis (doc 125). When a regulator or law-enforcement agency sends a requisition with a deadline during an incident, the bulk of the pain is coordinating many teams to produce the exact records each item asks for, on time. Each template is a ready structure: sections, each owned by a team, each item a question + the record to attach. `./securax crisis` opens a run from a template, assigns each item to its owner, tracks what is done vs pending vs overdue against the deadline, and generates the response pack. This is a STARTING library, deliberately generic (no organisation, person, address, IP or case number in it) — add your own agencies and items; it is data, no code change. Tiers: state (law-enforcement / police), national (sectoral CERT, central bank, national cyber agency), global (information-sharing bodies). Nothing here is legal advice; your legal and compliance teams own the actual response.

1.3.why: a ready duty-roster template to fill from HR/attendance records

8.3.why: the incident escalation timeline the estate already keeps

a.2.why: the scope note and time-wise action log pattern

c.1.why: the collection order of work (volatile first, hash everything)

c.2.why: the estate's own triage collectors and read-me card

k.1.why: the chain-of-custody form, one per artefact

k.2.why: the custody record and SHA-256 manifest the estate produces

r.1.why: the incident facts and status, timestamped

r.2.why: the IOC list the estate already holds

r.3.why: the containment actions recorded on the clock

i.1.why: the confirmed facts and current status

d.1.why: the timeline from first anomaly to containment

d.3.why: the register of notifications made to every agency

z.1.why: the root-cause weakness and its fix-by date

z.2.why: the blameless postmortem seeded with the timeline

le-production-notice.name: Law-enforcement production notice
le-production-notice.about: A police / state cyber agency production-or-appearance notice (e.g. a summons for documents under the local criminal-procedure code) after a payment-fraud complaint. Typically a long schedule of questions, each needing a specific record from a specific team, within a short deadline. Generalised from a real drill.

items.q: Org chart of every team that handles the payment rail (payments cell, treasury/settlement, back office, IT application, middleware, server, database, network, information security, SOC), with names as on the incident date.
Head of each team and their reporting officer.
Shift-wise duty roster for each team over the incident window: shift timings, persons rostered and who actually attended.
Who was on night / weekend / holiday duty, and anyone on duty outside their normal shift.
Anyone on leave, tour, work-from-home or newly posted; who stood in, and did the stand-in use their own user ID.
Who was on call / standby for each team; were they contacted, and by whom.
items.record: On-call list; call logs of official phones

items.q: Staff who joined, transferred in/out, resigned or retired from these teams in the period.
The normal maker-checker flow for an outward payment, from branch/entity entry to signing and release; who acts at each step.
Every user who held maker, checker, authoriser or signing rights in the core and rail applications during the window, with role and access level.
For each disputed message: maker ID, checker ID, signer ID / certificate, terminal or IP, and timestamp at each step; if a field is blank, say so.
Who logged in to the rail screens in the period: login/logout time, terminal and IP per session.
Which signing certificates or HSM keys signed the disputed messages; custodian of each, where kept, who held the PIN.
Were any disputed messages approved in bulk, by an auto-approval rule, or by a system / service account; name the account and who controls it.
Were any maker-checker limits, approval rules or straight-through settings changed shortly before the incident; who requested, approved and made the change.
Did any one person act as both maker and checker, or use another person's ID, in this period.
Every user of the secure-messaging member interface (operator, verifier, authoriser, security officer) with ID and rights during the window.
Who logged in to the messaging interface in the period, from which terminal / IP, for how long.
Who holds the administrator and security-officer roles; who can create users and reset passwords.
Were any messaging users created, unlocked, reset or re-privileged near the incident; by whom.
The bank's contact person with the rail operator; did anyone call or email the operator during the window.
items.record: Call and email records with the operator

items.q: Administrators of the rail gateway, integration broker, message queue and dispatcher during the window (staff or vendor), with user IDs.
Who could put, browse, move or delete messages on the rail queues.
Who logged in to the middleware / gateway consoles in the period, from where and when.
Any deployment, patch, script, flow or configuration change to these applications shortly before the incident; who made it and who approved it.
Any scripts, batch jobs or schedulers that write to the rail application or queues that ran in the period; who owns each.
Who knows the service-account passwords used by the gateway/middleware, and when they were last changed.
All servers in the rail chain (hostname, OS, IP, location) and their OS administrators.
Who had root / administrator / sudo rights on these servers during the window.
Who logged in to these servers in the period, from which IP, and what commands they ran.
items.record: OS login & shell history; PAM session recordings

items.q: DBAs for the rail and core databases, with DB user IDs; which DB accounts could INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE the rail tables; is the application account's password known to any individual.
Any direct SQL, data-fix or back-end update run on the rail or core database during the window; who ran it, under which approval.
Were DB or OS audit logs switched off, purged, rotated early or edited in this period; who has rights to do so.
Any backups, restores or DR drills run in the period; who ran them.
Network and firewall administrators on duty during the window.
SOC analysts and SOC manager on each shift; is the SOC in-house or outsourced.
Did the SOC raise any alert on the rail servers, queues, messaging or privileged accounts in this period; who saw it and what was done.
Who used VPN, jump servers or PAM to reach the rail systems in this period: user, source IP, time and target.
Any firewall rules, VPN accounts or remote-access tools (remote-desktop software) added or changed shortly before the incident; by whom.
The CISO and information-security officers; when were they told of the incident, and by whom.
Any user IDs on the rail chain shared by more than one person, or generic (admin/root/support/test); who knows their passwords.
Every user ID created, re-activated, unlocked, given higher rights or password-reset in the run-up to the incident; who requested and who approved each.
IDs of staff who left, transferred or are on long leave but are still active.
Any user ID used from two locations or terminals at the same time, or outside office hours.
When was the last user-access review for these systems; who signed it, and were any findings left open.
Who does the daily reconciliation of the rail settlement account; who did it on each day of the window and at what time.
Who first noticed the mismatch, at what time, and whom they told.
Timeline from first notice onward of who was informed, when, and what each person decided.
Why outward payments were not stopped after the mismatch was noticed; who had authority to stop them, and was this considered.
Who decided the timing of the complaint to police and the report to the regulator.
Who requested recalls / holds from beneficiary banks, and when; which banks responded.

sections.title: Vendors, outsourced staff and connected entities

items.q: Every vendor / outsourced firm supporting the core, rail, databases, network or SOC, and the staff deployed, with user IDs.
Which vendor staff worked on-site or remotely during the window; times and access method.
Any vendor staff who joined, left or were replaced in the period.
Connected sub-entities (correspondent/sponsored entities) able to create rail requests, and how they log in.
The incident-response firm under the cyber-insurance cover, its subcontractor, and every person from them who accessed systems since the incident, with dates and actions.
items.record: Engagement letters; IR access log; evidence-handover records

items.q: Who entered the data centre, DR site, rail cell and server rooms during the window; entry and exit times.
Preserve CCTV footage of these areas for the window; who has custody of it.
Desktops, laptops and terminals used by the persons named; have any been formatted, reissued or sent for repair since the incident.
Were USB ports, personal devices or mobile hotspots allowed in these areas; any data-loss-prevention alerts in the period.
Has any named person faced disciplinary action, a vigilance case or an audit finding in the last five years.
Has any named person taken leave, resigned, sought transfer or stopped attending since the incident.
Did any named person report a phishing email, lost phone, stolen ID card or shared password before or during this period.
Has any staff member or vendor raised a concern or complaint about rail operations or access in the last year.

sections.title: Network connectivity, whitelisting and report server

items.q: Every IP address and range whitelisted with the rail operator for the messaging and rail links, for both DC and DR, as on the incident date.
items.record: IP-whitelisting forms and letters exchanged with the operator

items.q: Which servers/devices use each whitelisted IP (gateway, HSM, routers); the NAT mapping and firewall rules for each.
Any IP added, removed or changed in the whitelist in the period; who requested and approved it.
items.record: Change requests to the operator; approvals

items.q: The source IP of each disputed message as recorded at the bank's gateway; was every message sent from a whitelisted IP.
Which certificates or keys are registered with the operator; custodian of each.

The report server (hostname, IP, OS, application, connected databases, DC/DR, purpose); which reports it produces and who receives them; did the reports for the incident days show the disputed messages — if not, why.
items.record: Server inventory extract; report list & schedule; reports as generated

items.q: Who viewed, downloaded or exported rail reports during the window.
For each account in the disputed messages: is it a customer, office/GL, settlement, connected-entity or non-existent account; account number, name, type, branch, date opened, status.
items.record: Account list mapped to transaction references; account master extract

items.q: Who created each account, in which system, and when; maker and checker IDs, terminal and IP.
For customer accounts: opening form, KYC documents, approving officer. For office/GL: the approval note and authorising officer.
Was any such account created, re-activated or changed (name, limits, rail-enabled flag, mandate, linked mobile) in the run-up; by whom.
Why do the debits not appear in core banking; the accounting entries posted and the accounts actually debited.
Were the same accounts used in any rail message before the incident window; statements for each account for the period.

sectoral-cert-forensics.name: Sectoral / national CERT forensic-artefact requisition
sectoral-cert-forensics.about: A national or sectoral CERT asks for forensic artefacts from the affected systems within a short window (often 6 hours for the first report, then follow-ups). The pain is running the right collectors with proper authority and chain-of-custody without disturbing a running production system. Pair with the forensic-collection SOP, the tool-exception form and the chain-of-custody template.

items.q: Nature of the incident, systems affected, time of detection, current status.
Indicators of compromise observed so far (IPs, domains, hashes, accounts).
Immediate containment actions taken.

sections.title: Authority to collect on production systems

items.q: Written, time-boxed approval to run forensic collectors from external media on the named production servers, with admin access, server administrator present, output only to approved media.
items.record: Tool-exception / policy-exception form (see crisis doc forensic-tool-exception)

items.q: Scope and read-only assurance: no other change is made to the servers; all actions are time-logged.
Volatile data first (memory, running processes, network connections, logged-on users) before any shutdown.
Targeted triage artefacts (system, security and application event logs, registry/hives, scheduled tasks, services, prefetch, browser and PowerShell history) using an approved triage collector.
items.record: Triage package with SHA-256 per file

items.q: Application, gateway, messaging, database-audit and firewall/gateway logs for the incident window.
Disk image where required, taken with a write-blocker or forensically-sound method.
A signed chain-of-custody form for every artefact: what, when, by whom, hash, and each handover.
Secure handover of the artefacts to the CERT / IR firm, with a verifiable hash manifest.

regulator-incident-report.name: Financial-regulator incident report
regulator-incident-report.about: The financial regulator's incident-reporting obligation (an initial report within hours, a detailed report and a root-cause/closure report later). Deadlines and channels vary by jurisdiction; the incident clock (./securax incident) tracks the exact times. This template is the content the regulator typically wants.

items.q: What happened, when detected, systems and services affected, customer impact, current status.
Whether critical services (payments, customer channels) are up, degraded or down, and the workaround.
Timeline from first anomaly to containment; decisions and who took them.
Attack vector and extent, data/funds affected, and recovery actions.
Notifications made to other agencies (CERT, police, card networks, insurer) and their references.
Root cause, the control that failed, and the permanent fix with a date.
Lessons and the drill/test that will prove it stays fixed.
